name: Burgruine Kropfsberg
kurzbeschreibung: The Burgruine Kropfsberg near Brixlegg: powerful 13th-century three-tower fortress of the Salzburg Archbishops at the junction of the Inntal and Zillertal.
beschreibung:
Overview

The monumental Burgruine Kropfsberg rises on a prominent, wooded moraine hill in the hamlet of St. Gertraudi within the municipality of Reith im Alpbachtal, directly opposite the market town of Brixlegg. Situated at the strategically decisive confluence of the Zillertal and the wide lower Inn valley, this fortification served for centuries as the military and administrative stronghold of the Archbishopric of Salzburg against the neighbouring County of Tyrol. With its three distinctive defensive towers, expansive curtain walls, and commanding valley location, Kropfsberg ranks among the largest and most historic castle complexes in western Austria.

History & Military Architecture

The fortress dates back to the first half of the 13th century: commissioned around 1220 by the assertive Archbishop of Salzburg Eberhard II., construction began on a powerful border stronghold to defend rich Salzburg territories in the Zillertal and Unterinntal from Tyrolean incursions. The layout reflects high-medieval military engineering: three autonomous towers were erected on the castle plateau. The architectural centrepiece is the massive, circular Bergfried (keep) of quarry stone masonry, serving as the ultimate refuge in times of siege. Beside it, a square gate tower and the stately palas residential tower guarded the access. In 1427, Kropfsberg achieved major political significance: following bitter territorial conflicts, the Tyrolean sovereign Friedrich IV. mit der leeren Tasche and Salzburg Archbishop Eberhard III. von Neuhaus met here to sign the historic Kropfsberger Frieden (Peace of Kropfsberg), which settled the border along the Zillertal for generations. As judicial administration was relocated to Rattenberg and Zell am Ziller in the 16th century, the fortress lost its military function and fell into disrepair. At the dawn of the 20th century, the Seidl von Hohenvelden family acquired the estate and rescued the towers from imminent collapse through structural preservation. Over recent decades, the ruins have been carefully conserved.

Visit & Getting There

The grounds of the castle ruins and the viewing platforms on the hill are freely accessible year-round and free of charge (the private interior spaces of the restored living quarters are not open to the public). Arrival by car: via the Inntalautobahn A12, exit Kramsach/Alpbachtal, follow the B171 to Brixlegg and cross the Inn bridge into St. Gertraudi; parking is available in St. Gertraudi near the parish church or at the castle inn. From there, a signposted, shaded forest trail leads up to the castle gate in about ten minutes on foot. By public transport: take the ÖBB train to Brixlegg railway station, then continue by regional bus (line 4074) to St. Gertraudi or walk directly in about 15 minutes.

Tips

The forest trail to the castle ruins is a natural path requiring sturdy footwear; all-terrain prams can manage the ascent with some effort. From the plateau in front of the keep, visitors enjoy panoramic vistas of the Rofan mountains, the entrance to the Zillertal, and the castles of Lichtenwerth and Matzen in the valley below. Combine your excursion with a stroll through the picturesque Matzen castle park on the opposite bank of the Inn.
